title: Subqueries — scalar, correlated, APPLY operators, EXISTS vs IN
exp: Subqueries test your understanding of SQL execution and NULL semantics. The NOT IN NULL trap is a real production bug waiting to happen. CROSS APPLY and OUTER APPLY unlock the 'top N per group' pattern that trips up many candidates.
pts: Scalar subquery: returns exactly one value, usable anywhere a single value is expected (SELECT, WHERE, HAVING)
Non-correlated subquery: independent of outer query, executes once, result reused
Correlated subquery: references outer query columns, **re-executes for every outer row** — potentially O(n × m)
`EXISTS` short-circuits at first match; `IN` materialises the full result set first — EXISTS is usually faster for large sets
**NOT IN NULL trap:** if the subquery returns ANY NULL, NOT IN evaluates to UNKNOWN for every row → zero rows returned. Three-valued logic in action.
**NOT EXISTS** does not have the NULL trap — it checks for absence of matching rows and handles NULLs correctly
**CROSS APPLY:** correlated join to a table expression; preserves all outer rows that produce at least one inner row (like INNER JOIN)
**OUTER APPLY:** correlated join that preserves all outer rows even if inner expression returns nothing (like LEFT JOIN)
Top-N per group with APPLY: apply a `SELECT TOP N ... WHERE id = outer.id ORDER BY ...` per outer row — cleaner than a CTE with window functions for some patterns
Rewrite correlated subqueries to JOINs or window functions for better performance at scale
code:
-- NOT IN NULL trap: returns zero rows if any customer_id is NULL!
SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);  -- ❌ dangerous

-- Safe alternative 1: NOT EXISTS
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id); -- ✓

-- Safe alternative 2: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;  -- ✓ also works

-- Correlated subquery: employees earning > dept average
SELECT name, salary, dept FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
  WHERE dept = e.dept  -- correlated: re-runs for each outer row
);
-- Faster rewrite using window function:
SELECT name, salary, dept FROM (
  SELECT *, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
) t WHERE salary > dept_avg;

-- CROSS APPLY: most recent order per customer
SELECT c.id, c.name, latest.order_date, latest.total
FROM customers c
CROSS APPLY (
  SELECT TOP 1 order_date, total
  FROM orders WHERE customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY order_date DESC
) latest;

-- EXISTS vs IN: EXISTS is faster when subquery is large
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1000);

qa.q: What is the NOT IN NULL trap and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If a subquery used with NOT IN returns any NULL, then every row in the outer query evaluates to UNKNOWN (due to three-valued logic) and is filtered out — returning zero rows total. Fix: use NOT EXISTS instead, which checks for the absence of matching rows and handles NULLs correctly. Alternatively, add WHERE col IS NOT NULL to the subquery, but NOT EXISTS is safer and clearer.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

qa.q: When should you use EXISTS over IN and why?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** EXISTS short-circuits — it stops as soon as it finds the first matching row. IN materialises the entire result set. For large subquery results, EXISTS is typically faster. EXISTS also handles NULLs correctly (no NULL trap). Use IN when: the subquery result is small, you want a list of static values (IN (1,2,3)), or the NOT IN case when you've confirmed no NULLs exist.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.q: How would you rewrite a correlated subquery for better performance?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Most correlated subqueries can be rewritten as: (1) a JOIN with aggregation in a derived table or CTE, or (2) a window function. Example: instead of WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = e.dept), use AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) in a subquery/CTE then filter in the outer query. Window functions are usually faster because they make a single pass over the data.

qa.q: What is the difference between CROSS APPLY and CROSS JOIN?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CROSS JOIN combines two independent tables — neither side can reference the other. CROSS APPLY executes an inner table expression FOR EACH row of the outer table, and that expression CAN reference outer columns. This makes CROSS APPLY essential for calling table-valued functions per row, or for top-N per group queries where the inner SELECT uses a TOP N ... WHERE id = outer.id pattern.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What are the three ways to write "find customers who have never placed an order"?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1) NOT EXISTS (safest): WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id). 2) LEFT JOIN + IS NULL: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL. 3) NOT IN (risky): WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) — fails silently if customer_id can be NULL. Prefer NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN.
